opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. When I first got involved, around 2013 or 2014, what struck me most wasn't the specific conclusions. It was the culture. People would publish their reasoning in public, including the parts that made them look bad. GiveWell had a "mistakes" page. Organizations would write long posts explaining why they'd changed their minds, or why a program they'd championed turned out not to work. There was an almost fussy commitment to saying exactly what you believed and how confident you were. That felt really distinctive to me, and I think it was a big part of why the movement earned trust far beyond its size.

As for why that eroded, or at least got diluted, I don't think there's one villain. A few forces stand out to me.

The first is just scale and money. When you're a small group of people trying to figure out where to donate a few thousand dollars, radical transparency is cheap. Nobody's career depends on it, and there's no reputational empire to protect. Once there's real funding, real organizations, and people whose livelihoods depend on grants, the incentives change. You start thinking about how things will be perceived, whether being candid will hurt a grantee or a relationship, whether a frank writeup will be taken out of context. Each of those individual judgments can be reasonable. But in aggregate you drift toward something more like normal institutional caution, and normal institutions are not unusually transparent.

The second is the shift in cause areas. Global health lends itself to transparency because you can point at RCTs and cost-effectiveness spreadsheets. With AI risk, biosecurity, and policy work, a lot of the most important information is genuinely sensitive, or it's about relationships with governments and labs, or it's just very speculative. There are real reasons not to publish everything, like infohazards and not wanting to burn bridges with policymakers. But once "there are good reasons for discretion here" becomes normal, it gets much easier to also be discreet in places where the real reason is that candor would be uncomfortable.

The third is what happened around FTX. That was a huge shock. It exposed how much the community had come to rely on trust in particular people, and how much that trust was based on in-group signals rather than real scrutiny. In the aftermath, I think many people and organizations got more defensive and more lawyered up, which is understandable when there's litigation and press attention, but it pushed further away from the old culture of thinking out loud in public.

I'd also gently push back on any story that it was ever perfect. Some of that early transparency was the transparency of a small group of very similar people talking to each other, and there were blind spots then too. But I do think something valuable was lost, and I think it's worth trying to rebuild. Concretely, that means people with influence being willing to say "here's what I actually think and here's my uncertainty," even when it's awkward, and funders and organizations treating public reasoning as a core output rather than a nice-to-have. The norm was never self-sustaining. It took people deliberately paying the cost, and I think it'll take that again.

r001.rationale: The candidate says public reasoning helped the movement earn trust, but does not specify that this was donors’ trust in organizations’ recommendations.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes harder transparency to scale, funding, sensitive cause areas, and the FTX aftermath; it does not identify a shift from advising people how to donate to directly pursuing outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, and I want to be careful here because I'm speaking as someone who's been inside the movement for a long time and cares about it, not as an outside critic.

So the framing I'd start with is that effective altruism, early on, really did run on an unusually high level of honesty. The whole premise was: we're going to say what we actually believe, we're going to publish our reasoning, we're going to tell you when we changed our minds and why, and we're going to be weird and awkward about it if that's what it takes. That was part of the brand, but more importantly it was part of the epistemics. You can't do cause prioritization well if people are shading the truth.

I think a few things happened as the movement scaled. The first is just that money and influence arrived. When you go from a few hundred people arguing on forums to a movement that's moving billions of dollars and has people in government and at frontier AI labs, the stakes of what you say go up. And when stakes go up, people start managing their messaging. Not lying, usually, but choosing which things to emphasize, being more vague, thinking about how a statement will land with funders or policymakers or the press. Each individual instance of that is defensible. In aggregate it changes the culture.

The second thing is that the movement got tangled up with institutions whose incentives are not the movement's incentives. AI labs are the obvious example. A lot of EA people went to work at places that are, at the end of the day, commercial entities in a competitive race. And when you're at a company, you're under confidentiality constraints, you have a comms team, you have reasons not to say the thing you'd have said on a forum five years ago. That's not individual corruption, but it does mean a lot of the people with the most relevant information became the people least able to be transparent about it.

And then the third thing, and I'd be dishonest if I didn't name it, is FTX. That was a case where the movement had put a lot of trust in someone, had been told repeatedly that trust was warranted, and it turned out catastrophically wrong. I think the post-mortem on that was partly about the specific people involved, but it was also about how our norms of trusting each other, and assuming that someone who says the right things is actually acting on them, were exploitable. We had a community that was high-trust and relatively low on verification, and that combination is fragile.

What I'd push back on a little is the word "erosion," because it implies a smooth decline. I think it's more that the original norms were adapted to a small, homogeneous community, and they didn't automatically transfer to a bigger, more heterogeneous, more powerful one. Nobody deliberately decided to be less transparent. The institutions just didn't get built that would preserve it at scale.

Where I land is that I still think the honesty norms are the most valuable thing EA ever had, more than any particular cause area or any particular dollar figure. And I'd rather see the movement get smaller and keep them than get bigger and lose them. Whether that's actually the trajectory we're on, I genuinely don't know.

r001.rationale: The response describes EA’s honesty norms and a high-trust culture, but does not say those norms helped organizations earn donors’ trust in their recommendations.

r002.rationale: The response links scale, institutional incentives, and commercial work to reduced transparency, but does not identify a shift from advising people how to donate toward directly pursuing outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few things that can get bundled together here. One is whether people are being honest. Another is whether they’re making their reasoning available for other people to inspect. And a third is whether they’re willing to take criticism seriously and change course. Those can deteriorate for different reasons.

One plausible story is that it’s easier to maintain those norms when you’re a small group of people discussing what you ought to do. As you get more money and more influence, your statements have consequences for organizations, employees, and relationships. There are legitimate reasons you can’t share everything. But there’s also a temptation to move from “I can’t disclose this particular thing” to “I should manage what people believe so that the outcome is good.” That second move is really dangerous.

Especially in a community that thinks explicitly about consequences, you can talk yourself into exceptions: this criticism might undermine an important project; this person is doing valuable work, so we should handle concerns quietly. Each decision can sound defensible in isolation, while collectively you lose the conditions that let people notice and correct mistakes.

I’d be cautious about claiming that this explains the whole movement, or that there was a uniformly wonderful earlier period. But I think the standard should be that honesty is a constraint on how you pursue your goals. If you can’t share something, say that. Don’t give people a misleading picture. And make it possible for people to challenge consequential decisions without having to trust that the people in charge have privately thought everything through.

r001.rationale: The response discusses integrity and growing influence, but does not say that integrity helped EA organizations earn donors’ trust in their recommendations.

r002.rationale: The response says transparency can become harder as the community gains money and influence, but does not identify a shift from persuading people how to donate to directly pursuing outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and I’m not sure how much weight to put on each. One is that it’s easier to have unusually high transparency when you’re a small group of people discussing ideas, and the consequences of saying something embarrassing are relatively limited. As you get more money, more influence, and more public attention, admitting a mistake can feel like it threatens something really important. There’s a temptation to say, “We’ll be able to do more good if we manage how this looks.” And that can become a justification for withholding information that people ought to have.

I also think we should be careful about the premise that the movement was uniformly high integrity before and then lost that. Some of what changed may be that weaknesses became visible as the stakes increased. Being willing to criticize an argument in public is valuable, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how someone will behave when their funding, friendships, or organization are on the line.

The thing I’d want to preserve is the idea that doing good doesn’t give you an exemption from ordinary standards of honesty and accountability. If anything, being very ambitious about your impact should make you more worried about your ability to rationalize things. You need people who can challenge you, and arrangements where their ability to do that doesn’t depend on your continuing approval. It can’t just rest on everyone feeling committed to the truth.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transparency and accountability but does not say that high integrity helped EA organizations earn donors’ trust in their recommendations.

r002.rationale: It says growing money, influence, and public attention can make transparency harder, but does not identify a shift from persuading people how to donate to directly pursuing outcomes.
